title: Requirements and Back-of-Envelope Estimation
summary: Turn a vague prompt into numbers you can design against, without pretending the estimates are exact.
keyPoints: Functional requirements define what the system does; non-functional requirements define how well it must do it.
Estimate reads, writes, storage, and bandwidth from daily users and per-user actions.
Average QPS is not peak QPS; peak is often 2-5x average for consumer systems.
State assumptions and round aggressively. The goal is the right order of magnitude.
Availability and latency targets determine replication, caching, and timeout budgets.

complexity.note: Use seconds per day for requests.

commonMistakes: Designing for average QPS without a peak estimate.
Forgetting replication and index overhead when estimating storage.
Treating an availability target as free; each additional nine adds complexity and cost.
Changing the assumptions halfway through without updating the numbers.
interviewNotes: Write the formula, not just the result, so the interviewer can follow your reasoning.
Ask whether the read-to-write ratio is known; it changes the caching and replication strategy.
If you are unsure, give a range and say which end you would design for.

checkYourself.question: Why is peak QPS more important than average QPS for capacity planning?
checkYourself.answer: The system must survive the busiest moment. Provisioning for the average leaves it overloaded during peaks.

checkYourself.question: How many seconds are in a day, rounded for estimation?
checkYourself.answer: About 86,400. Round to 100,000 when a rough estimate is enough.

checkYourself.question: What does 99.9% availability mean in downtime per month?
checkYourself.answer: About 43 minutes per month, assuming a 30-day month.
